items.title: Joe Watkins Interview, 1960-03-16
items.q: when Bud Russel came out and heard me one night, right a few blocks up here on Galvest Street on a Sunday night, brought his bass along. So that made us have three pieces

ctx.x: When you were a kid, did you play on any toy drums or beat on anything?

No, no, no. I didn't beat on it. All I beat it on was the bottom of my mother's old wash tub or upside the fence, yeah. Yeah. So around 1918 I went to work at the Whitney National Bank as a night port. At that time they had Bud Russel, I know you know him. I've heard him. Ed Darcy was working there. Well Ed Darcy's still with him, yeah, but Bud Russel died. Well I was playing piano with a boyfriend of mine named Shedrick Brewster, but we called him nicknamed Baby Brewster, and we used to play house parties on…
What style? Was it something like Baby Dodds or anything particular about his style you could tell us?

items.title: Joe Watkins Interview, 1969-03-24
items.q: So I played out there with them and, uh, a fella called Dude and his brother.

ctx.x: Okay, well we're interviewing Joe Watkins this March 24th, 1969. Just going from what you're about to say, Joe, about when you started music.

When I started, I started in 1920s. Well that was quite a few years after George Lewis and Paul Barbrain. Well I always did love drums because I was born in the third ward and that was, a section for jazz probably because Lee Armstrong was from that ward. He was born and raised around there. And I don't know about Joe Oliver because I always heard that Joe was not exactly from the Orlins. But it was him, Lee Armstrong, Funk Johnson, and you had Manuel Moneta. And, uh, was this other fella's name, uh, was a good…
What sort of date was this? Huh? What date was this about?
